dossier.architecture: Turreted shooter with physics-based moving shots and truss-reacting traversal climb.

subsystems.drivetrain: Custom swerve; slip detection reduces trust in wheel odometry.
subsystems.intake: Rigid collector with elastic linkage that yields inward on impact.
subsystems.transfer: Separate horizontal and vertical conveyors; infrared/color sensors track cargo.
subsystems.scoring: Low-mounted two-motor turret transmission; adjustable hood and later top roller.
subsystems.endgame: Telescopic hook plus truss-reaction structure reaches traversal with few active steps; deployable line camera improves alignment.
subsystems.controls: Shot simulation selects trajectories insensitive to error; fused pose and radial/tangential velocity compensation support moving shots.

versions: Shooter rebuilt after first Israeli event to add top roller and reduce bounce-outs. Alignment camera added after approach time became a climb bottleneck.
dossier.analysis: Their advantage is the combined localization, shot model and mechanically repeatable feeder. A turret alone does not create accurate moving shots; alignment time can dominate an otherwise fast climber.
limits: Reported performance and prototype history are attributed to the source; not every intermediate revision is recoverable.

context_documents.title: 2022-1690 · Moving shots require a state model beyond distance alone
context_documents.body:
# 2022-1690: Moving shots require a state model beyond distance alone

Focused study supplement. Not a full binder/CAD review, exhaustive subsystem specification, every-version history or visual interview watch.

## Published / retained construction account

A compliant-link collector feeds horizontal/vertical conveyors and a low-driven turret. The source describes a shot model using distance and chassis velocity components to select hood angle and wheel speed.

## Team-stated reasoning or boundary

The retained construction uses linkage compliance for impact survival; the interview explains compensating radial and tangential motion in the aiming solution.

## Engineering interpretation — analyst inference

A distance-only lookup cannot describe the same shot from a stationary robot and one moving sideways. The compensation still depends on measured release behavior and pose latency. A sophisticated model does not excuse uncontrolled incoming cargo state.

## Proposed validation — not performed

Test moving-shot error by direction/speed, camera latency and worn cargo; compare predicted and measured flight time.

## Limits

Focused technical passages and the retained dossier are the evidence scope. Exact event installation, complete CAD tolerances and all intermediate revisions are not certified.

source_reviews.title: Behind the Bumpers with Orbit at Championship
source_reviews.locator: 1:37–3:05 drive and intake; 3:12–5:26 conveyors and turret; 5:30–7:50 climb; 8:00–12:06 shot model and state estimation
source_reviews.review_basis: Read the full available English automatic caption track, including the start and end. Technical details are attributed to team speakers. No visual inspection claimed.
facts: Rigid intake arms yield rearward through surgical tubing in the deployment linkage.
The turret gearbox sits low and transmits torque up the structure. A new shooter with a top roller followed observed bounce-outs.
The climb reacts against the truss and uses a deployed line camera. The team models moving shots and combines encoders, gyro and vision for pose.
source_reviews.limitations: These are descriptions of the championship machine and earlier revisions. The calibration, model source code and shot statistics were not reviewed.

source_reviews.title: Orbit introduces Parker
source_reviews.review_basis: Read team reveal text and attachment metadata.
facts: Names Parker and announces the first and third Israel district events.
source_reviews.limitations: Attachment located, with no visual mechanism verification.

source_review.whole_robot_explanation: Parker joined a rigid collection mechanism to a deliberately yielding deployment, and a wide-yaw shooter to an estimator that could account for chassis motion. Both choices move the hardest problems to interfaces. The intake needs to fold without losing the capture geometry after impact. The shooter needs fresh velocity and a model that predicts the ball’s behavior over a range of entry conditions.
piece_flow: The collector captures the ball and shares its drive with the horizontal conveyor.
A separate vertical drive meters cargo to the shooter. Three infrared positions and color sensing track staged balls.
The hood, top roller and main launcher release while turret aim and shot setpoints compensate for robot motion.
source_review.packaging_and_motion: The team wanted low mass distribution and mounted the turret gearbox near the bottom, with torque sent up the tower. Printed guides manage the long cable as yaw passes through a full turn. The truss reactor sweeps outside its stowed volume, and deploys a small camera arm whose view of the floor line helps place the chassis before lift.

subsystems.name: Impact-tolerant collector
subsystems.construction: Rigid arms with a driven sprocket lever and surgical-tubing coupling.
subsystems.operation: Pull down to deploy. Under a rearward hit the assembly can yield and fold toward the robot.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team’s prior flexible intake worked but needed frequent replacement. It wanted rigidity in normal use without transmitting full impact to the motor and frame.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: A compliant actuator coupling can protect the drive while keeping the roller stiff. Verify that yielding stops short of belts, cables and hard structure.
subsystems.interfaces: After an impact the horizontal conveyor still needs its original entry geometry.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Test angled hits and repeatability after many folds. Inspect tubing for loss of force.
subsystems.unknowns: Actual release force and geometry unknown.

subsystems.name: Transport and turret launcher
subsystems.construction: Shared collector/horizontal drive, independent vertical conveyor, adjustable hood, added top roller and low-mounted turret drive.
subsystems.operation: Stage independently of the floor path. Set yaw and hood, then release with the intended wheel states.
subsystems.team_rationale: A top roller was added after early balls bounced out of the hub. The team describes dual turret motors for responsiveness under launcher motion.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Elevated cable drag and reflected inertia can change control across yaw. Measure release under speed and yaw changes rather than inferring it from static tuning.
subsystems.interfaces: The tower shaft, cable guides and moving ball entry have to remain aligned after service.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Check wire abrasion at limits, ball entry under yaw and top-wheel speed after consecutive launches.
subsystems.unknowns: Torque margin and measured spin remain open.

subsystems.name: Moving-shot controls
subsystems.construction: Trajectory simulation includes gravity, drag and Magnus force. The team describes selecting less sensitive combinations and correcting for chassis velocity. Pose estimation combines wheel encoders, gyro and vision.
subsystems.operation: Estimate radial and transverse motion, choose the shot and shift aim to compensate. The team also logs skids and limits reliance on drive estimates during them.
subsystems.team_rationale: A distance-by-velocity test grid was judged impractical. The team wanted a shot less sensitive to mechanical variation.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Compare model residuals under representative wear and speeds. A low-sensitivity choice in the model only helps if it matches actual release behavior.
subsystems.interfaces: Targeting and pose share vision and velocity estimates.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Exercise skid, delayed vision and a rapid acceleration immediately before release.
subsystems.unknowns: No model coefficients, validation set or latency budget.

subsystems.name: Truss-reacting climb
subsystems.construction: Telescopic lift, V-shaped reactor, traversal hooks and a spring-deployed line camera on a small arm.
subsystems.operation: Lift while the reactor contacts the truss and changes body attitude. Capture traversal, then release the lower rung.
subsystems.team_rationale: The team wanted few actions and found initial alignment took a large share of total time.
subsystems.engineering_analysis: Using field contact saves actuation only if real approach error and field tolerances still allow the intended reaction.
subsystems.interfaces: Camera alignment must correspond to the hook and reactor pose, not just chassis heading.
subsystems.service_and_failure_modes: Try lateral offsets, missed floor line and contact near truss joints.
subsystems.unknowns: Measured load and capture margins unresolved.

revisions: Shooter replaced after the first Israeli event. Team added climb alignment and reports later skid detection.
transferable_principles: Include approach time in climb optimization.
Use model-based compensation where input quality and repeatable release justify it.
disconfirming_conditions: If field contact is unavailable or inconsistent, the reactor geometry loses its simplifying benefit.
Variable piece properties or noisy speed estimates can undermine moving-shot compensation.
remaining_gaps: Geometry, measured shot validation and control source.

recommended_images.caption: Team reveal overview. Verify whether shooter predates the new upper roller.
